meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I don't give advice; I give opinions'?
meta.ogDescription: John Wooden really did say it. Bill Walton wrote it down in 1994 and Wooden used the exact line in a 1997 interview — but not from any book of his that anyone has cited.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1910–2010 · UCLA head basketball coach, winner of ten NCAA titles
answer.sourceLine: This one holds up. It was a spoken catchphrase rather than a line from any book Wooden wrote: his UCLA centre Bill Walton set it down as Wooden’s standing reply in the 1994 memoir Nothing But Net, and Quote Investigator ↗ documents Wooden using the identical words himself in The Indianapolis News of 28 March 1997. The wording that circulates uses a semicolon; every documented transcription uses a comma.

source.excerpt: If you asked him for advice, he would always say, “I don’t give advice, I give opinions.”
trail: 1994 — Bill Walton publishes Nothing But Net ↗ with Gene Wojciechowski (Hyperion, New York), recording the sentence as the answer Wooden gave anyone who asked him for advice. Quote Investigator verified the pages with scans.

20 February 1994 — the Lexington Herald-Leader runs a piece by Jerry Tipton in which Wooden explains why he shies from telling younger coaches what to do: he can give an opinion, and that is a big difference (citation via Quote Investigator ↗).
28 March 1997 — Bill Benner in The Indianapolis News quotes Wooden on UCLA coach Steve Lavin using the exact wording — the earliest instance in Wooden’s own voice that Quote Investigator ↗ documents.
2025 — Quote Investigator ↗ assembles the chain and concludes that Wooden did employ the quotation.
source.excerptNote: Bill Walton, Nothing But Net (Hyperion, 1994), chap. 2, pp. 20–21, in a passage about Wooden treating basketball as a microcosm of life. Three years later Wooden used the line himself, telling The Indianapolis News about his conversations with UCLA coach Steve Lavin: “I don’t give advice, I give opinions … on whatever he asks.”

author.name: John Wooden
author.kicker: The coach who refused to be didactic
author.heading: Who was John Wooden?
author.metaLine: 1910–2010 · American basketball coach & player, “the Wizard of Westwood”
author.bio: John Robert Wooden (1910–2010) coached the UCLA Bruins from 1948 to 1975 and won ten NCAA national championships in twelve years, including a record seven in a row — a run no one has come near since. He thought of himself as a teacher first, and his practices doubled as sessions in method and character, which is why so many of his lines survive as maxims rather than as passages from any book. Younger coaches sought him out for decades after he retired, and the advice-versus-opinion distinction was how he kept those conversations from turning into instructions.

misattribution.heading: What gets garbled
misattribution.intro: The attribution is sound — this is one of the rare Wooden lines that survives contact with a fact-checker. What goes wrong is the punctuation and the paperwork.

items.why: The form that circulates — “I don’t give advice; I give opinions” — is punctuated with a semicolon, and even Quote Investigator’s own headline ↗ uses one. Every wording that page actually transcribes from a 1990s source, Walton’s and Wooden’s alike, uses a comma.

Quote collections file the line under Wooden with no citation at all — the reader who wrote to Quote Investigator ↗ said flatly that no solid citation could be found. Every instance anyone has produced is spoken: preserved by a player who heard it and by reporters who wrote it down. It does not appear among Wikiquote’s sourced selections from his books either.

misattribution.truthLine: Wooden really said it. Quote Investigator ↗ documents him using the exact sentence in his own voice about UCLA coach Steve Lavin in The Indianapolis News of 28 March 1997 — three years after Bill Walton’s 1994 memoir had already recorded it as his coach’s standing reply.

context.heading: Why the distinction mattered to him
lead: Wooden retired in 1975 and then spent thirty-five years being asked what to do. His answer was a rule about his own standing: he would not tell another coach how to run a team he had not watched. Talking to the Lexington Herald-Leader in February 1994 he set out the reasoning plainly — he did not know enough about the situation each coach faced to give advice, but he could give an opinion, and, as Quote Investigator ↗ transcribes it, “That’s a big difference.”

That is the whole point of the line, and it is why it reads as modesty rather than evasion. Advice implies the giver knows the answer; an opinion leaves the decision where it belongs. Bill Walton, who played for Wooden at UCLA from 1971 to 1974, remembered it as the reflex response to any request for guidance — the sentence you got before you got anything else.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator lists a 1996 column by Joyce Fittro, a home economics extension agent, in The Delaware Gazette of Ohio, which expresses the same idea about listening without crediting Wooden — a useful reminder that the sentiment circulated on its own even while Wooden was making it his signature.

When Wooden died in 2010, the Associated Press obituary quoted former UCLA coach Jim Harrick describing the same habit: he would never give advice, but he would always give opinions. Two witnesses sixteen years apart, describing the same reflex, is about as good as an oral catchphrase gets.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes John Wooden did employ "I don't give advice, I give opinions," citing Bill Walton's 1994 book Nothing But Net (chap. 2, pp. 20-21, Hyperion, New York, verified with scans); a 20 February 1994 Lexington Herald-Leader piece by Jerry Tipton in which Wooden says he can give an opinion and "That's a big difference"; a 17 February 1996 Delaware Gazette column by Joyce Fittro expressing the notion without crediting Wooden; a 28 March 1997 Indianapolis News piece by Bill Benner (quote page D2) quoting Wooden saying "I don't give advice, I give opinions ... on whatever he asks" about Steve Lavin; and a 2010 Associated Press obituary quoting Jim Harrick. QI's headline uses a semicolon while every transcribed wording uses a comma.

The Internet Archive holds a scanned, borrowable copy of Bill Walton's Nothing But Net: Just Give Me the Ball and Get Out of the Way, published New York: Hyperion, 1994, ISBN 1562827936, associated name Gene Wojciechowski.

John Robert Wooden lived 14 October 1910 to 4 June 2010, was nicknamed "the Wizard of Westwood," coached the UCLA Bruins from 1948 to 1975, and won ten NCAA national championships in a twelve-year period including a record seven in a row.

Wikiquote's John Wooden page contains no line about advice or opinions in any section; its sourced quotes come from They Call Me Coach (1972), Wooden: A Lifetime of Observations and Reflections (1997), a 2000 Charlie Rose interview and a 2003 IBM commercial, and its Misattributed section lists only "Failing to prepare is preparing to fail."
Bill Walton (5 November 1952 - 27 May 2024) played for UCLA under coach John Wooden from 1971 to 1974.
